**Jayne Anne Phillips** (born July 19, 1952)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-encyclopedia.com-1) is an American novelist and short story writer who was born in the small town of [Buckhannon, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckhannon,_West_Virginia "Buckhannon, West Virginia"). She was a professor of English at [Rutgers-Newark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers-Newark "Rutgers-Newark") from 2005 to 2020 and helped establish the MFA program at [Rutgers University-Newark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University-Newark "Rutgers University-Newark").
## Education
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education")]
Phillips graduated from [West Virginia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia_University "West Virginia University"), earning a [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.A. "B.A.") in 1974, and later received an [M.F.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Fine_Arts "Master of Fine Arts") in fiction from the [Iowa Writers' Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Writers'_Workshop "Iowa Writers' Workshop") at the [University of Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Iowa "University of Iowa").
## Teaching
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Teaching")]
Phillips has held teaching positions at several colleges and universities, including [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), [Williams College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_College "Williams College"), Brandeis University, and [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University"). She is currently Professor of English and founder/director of the [Rutgers University–Newark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University%E2%80%93Newark "Rutgers University–Newark") Master of Fine Arts in Creative Writing Program.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-2) In 2007, _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_ magazine named Phillips' MFA program at Rutgers–Newark in its list of "Five Up-and-Coming" creative writing programs in the United States.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-3)
## Writing career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Writing career")]
### Early career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early career")]
In the mid-1970s, Phillips left West Virginia for California, embarking on a cross-country trip in the course of which she had numerous jobs, experiences, and encounters that would greatly influence her fiction, with its focus on lonely, lost souls and struggling survivors.
In 1976, Truck Press published her first short story collection _Sweethearts_ , for which Phillips earned a [Pushcart Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pushcart_Prize "Pushcart Prize") and the Coordinating Council of Literary Magazines Fels Award.
_Sweethearts_ was followed in 1978 by a second small-press collection, _Counting_ , issued by Vehicle Editions. _Counting_ earned Phillips greater recognition and the St. Lawrence Award.
Her next collection, _[Black Tickets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Tickets "Black Tickets")_ , published by Delacorte/[Seymour Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delacorte_Press "Delacorte Press") in 1979 when she was 26, was her first book of stories and brought her national attention as a talented and important writer. _Black Tickets_ contained three types of stories: one-page fictions, inner soliloquies, and family dramas. These stories focused on the characters' loneliness, alienation, and unsuccessful search for happiness. _Black Tickets_ is mentioned in the 2006 lectures for the Modern Scholar series installment _From Here to Infinity_ , by Professor [Michael D. C. Drout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_D._C._Drout "Michael D. C. Drout"), who refers to her style —— he asserts it had a direct influence on [William Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gibson "William Gibson")'s 1984 [cyberpunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberpunk "Cyberpunk") novel _[Neuromancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromancer "Neuromancer")_ — as a "headlong rush of story and description".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-4) Called "the unmistakable work of early genius" by Tillie Olsen, _Black Tickets_ was praised by [Raymond Carver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Carver "Raymond Carver"): "These stories of America's disenfranchised – men and women light-years away from the American Dream – are quite unlike any in our literature ... this book is a crooked beauty." _Black Tickets_ was awarded the Sue Kaufman Prize for First Fiction by the [American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_and_Institute_of_Arts_and_Letters "American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In 1984, Phillips published her first novel, _Machine Dreams_ , "a remarkable novelistic debut and an enduring literary achievement," according to the [_New York Times_.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Times.?action=edit&redlink=1 "New York Times. \(page does not exist\)") _Machine Dreams_ is a chronicle of the Hampson family from World War II to the Vietnam War. A [National Book Critics Circle Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Critics_Circle_Award "National Book Critics Circle Award") Finalist in Fiction, it was named one of 12 Best Books of the Year cited by the _New York Times_. It appeared on several Bestseller lists and was optioned as a film by actor [Jessica Lange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Lange "Jessica Lange"), who wrote the screenplay. Nobel Prize winner [Nadine Gordimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadine_Gordimer "Nadine Gordimer") said that _Machine Dreams_ "reaches one's deepest emotions. No number of books read or films seen can deaden one to the intimate act of art by which this wonderful young writer has penetrated the definitive experience of her generation." _[Fast Lanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Lanes?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fast Lanes \(page does not exist\)")_ , a 1987 collection of ten stories, all first-person narratives, was praised as work by a writer "in love with the American language." One of the stories from _Fast Lanes_ , "Rayme," had been published in 1984 in _Granta'_ s [Dirty Realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirty_realism "Dirty realism") issue.
In 1994, Phillips published her second novel, _Shelter,_ a portrait of the loss of innocence at a West Virginia girls' camp in the summer of 1963. Called "a rich, vivid novel of moral and psychological complexity destined to stand alongside works by Faulkner and other Southern masters" (_Vanity Fair_) and "a defiant, frighteningly beautiful novel as disturbing as its setting, _Shelter_ feels like Phillips' bid for immortality" (_Harper's Bazaar_). Shelter was awarded an Academy Award in Literature by the American Academy and Institute of Arts and Letters.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
### Later career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later career")]
Phillips' next novel was _[MotherKind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MotherKind?action=edit&redlink=1 "MotherKind \(page does not exist\)")_ (2000), winner of the [Massachusetts Book Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Book_Award "Massachusetts Book Award"), a story of intergenerational love and struggles within a family facing many changes. It is praised as one of the best novels about mothers and infants and the mother/daughter bond.
_[Lark and Termite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lark_and_Termite?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lark and Termite \(page does not exist\)")_ , her fourth novel, was published by [Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf "Alfred A. Knopf") in 2009 to positive reviews and was selected as one of five finalists for the [National Book Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award "National Book Award") in fiction.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-rutgers-5) _Lark and Termite_ was also a Finalist for the National Book Critics Circle in Fiction; _Lark et Termite_ (French translation by Marc Amfreville) was a Finalist for the Prix de Medici Etrangers (Paris).
_Quiet Dell_ , Phillips' fifth novel, based on the true story of the 1931 murders of Chicago widow Asta Eicher and her three children in the hamlet of Quiet Dell, West Virginia, is a fictional portrayal of one of the nation's first sensationalized serial murders. _Quiet Dell_ takes as its protagonist nine-year-old Annabel Eicher (victim, with her family, of con man [Harry Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Powers "Harry Powers"), who found his victims through Depression-era matrimonial agencies) and Emily Thornhill, a _[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")_ journalist who commits herself to finding justice for the Eichers. A Kirkus Review Fiction Pick of the Year and _Wall Street Journal_ Best Book of the Year, _Quiet Dell_ was called "a story both splendid and irreparably sad" by the _Chicago Tribune_ : "As Phillips has proved throughout her decades of fiction writing, there is evil in the world but there are some who will stand in its way." _Quiet Dell_ was praised by the _Philadelphia Review of Books_ : "It is the texture of the telling that elevates this recounting from true crime to the realm of literary eminence."
Phillips' works have been translated and published in twelve foreign languages.
## Awards and honours
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jayne_Anne_Phillips&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards and honours")]
She is the recipient of a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship"), two [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts") Fellowships, a Bunting Fellowship from the Bunting Institute of [Radcliffe College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_College "Radcliffe College"), a Rockefeller Foundation Bellagio Fellowship, and numerous other awards. In 2024, she was awarded the [Pulitzer Prize for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Fiction "Pulitzer Prize for Fiction") for her novel _[Night Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_Watch_\(Phillips_novel\) "Night Watch \(Phillips novel\)")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_Anne_Phillips#cite_note-6)
